chunks: Sa'd ibn Abdillah from Abu Ja'far from Sa'd ibn Isma'il ibn Isa from his father who said:

I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who had janabah in the month of Ramadan and slept intentionally until morning. What is upon him? He said: 'This does not harm him, nor does it break his fast, and it does not matter, for my father (peace be upon him) said: 'Aisha said: Indeed the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) became junub from intercourse, not from wet dream.' There is nothing in this report that contradicts what we mentioned, because his saying 'a man who had janabah in the month of Ramadan and slept intentionally until morning' does not indicate that he intentionally left the ghusl; rather he said 'slept intentionally until morning', so he attributed the intentionality to the sleeping. There would only be doubt if he said 'intentionally left the ghusl', and it is permissible that he intentionally slept at the beginning of the night and remained sleeping until morning, at which time the kaffarah would not be obligatory upon him, and that is what he also narrated.

key_terms.جُنُب: One in the state of janabah

ai.seo_question: Does sleeping intentionally while junub in Ramadan break the fast and require kaffarah?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi highlights the critical jurisprudential distinction between intentionally remaining in a state of janabah versus intentionally sleeping to delay ghusl, ruling that the latter does not incur kaffarah. This is supported by the precedent of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) who was junub from intercourse and slept until morning, as reported by Aisha, demonstrating that the state of impurity itself does not nullify the fast. The text further clarifies that if one sleeps early and remains asleep until dawn, the delay in ghusl is not considered an intentional act of breaking the fast.
